title: 22. Interview: Eventual Consistency
summary: Interview Q&A for Eventual Consistency — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Eventual Consistency interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define eventual consistency and state its liveness and safety properties precisely.
**Answer:** Eventual consistency is the guarantee that if no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses will return the last written value. The liveness property is convergence: in a system where replicas communicate reliably and infinitely often, all replicas reach the same final state. The safety property is weak: during convergence, a read may return *any* value that the local replica has observed — including stale values, intermediate values, or values that will later be overwritten. There is no upper bound on the convergence time in the basic model; practical systems bound it operationally (DynamoDB typically sub-second, DNS minutes, anti-entropy cycles in Cassandra configurable from minutes to hours). The model also implicitly assumes eventual delivery (every write eventually reaches every replica) and eventual termination of conflicts (the conflict-resolution function is total). Note that eventual consistency does *not* guarantee that two reads issued at the same wall-clock time will agree — they may be from different replicas in different convergence states. Stronger variants add session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) and bounded staleness (e.g., "reads are at most 5 seconds stale") to tighten the safety property.
**Visual:**
```
liveness: no new writes -> all replicas converge (eventually)
safety  : during convergence, read may return ANY observed value
              (no bound in base model; practical systems add bound)
```

### Q2. Explain last-writer-wins (LWW). What are its failure modes and how do production systems mitigate them?
**Answer:** Last-writer-wins is a conflict-resolution policy where each write carries a timestamp and the write with the highest timestamp supersedes all earlier writes on convergence. Its advantage is mechanical simplicity: deterministic, automatic, no application code. Its failure modes are well-known. First, clock skew: if two replicas' NTP clocks disagree by 200ms, the write with the higher wall-clock timestamp wins regardless of which actually happened later, silently corrupting data. Production systems mitigate this by tightly bounding clock skew (NTP with GPS reference, Spanner's TrueTime, AWS's Time Sync Service) and by using hybrid logical clocks (HLCs) that combine wall-clock with a logical counter to break ties. Second, silent data loss: if two clients update the same shopping-cart item, the later write wins and the earlier one vanishes — the application never learns about the conflict. Mitigation is to design schemas so concurrent writes do not collide (use append-only events, immutable rows, or partition keys that disperse concurrent writers). Third, hot-key storms: a viral post's like counter at LWW can drop writes if many writers stamp the same key simultaneously. Mitigation is to use counters (a CRDT) rather than LWW for monotonically increasing values, or to shard the counter across many keys.
**Visual:**
```
client A: write(x=1, ts=100)  \
client B: write(x=2, ts=200)   } LWW picks x=2, x=1 silently lost
                                 (no application notification)
mitigation: HLC, schema design (append-only), CRDT for counters
```

### Q3. What is a vector clock and how does it detect concurrent writes?
**Answer:** A vector clock is a map from node-id to logical counter, maintained per replica. When a replica performs a local write, it increments its own counter in the vector. When it sends a message, it attaches its current vector; the receiver takes the per-component max of its own vector and the incoming vector, then increments its own counter. Two vector clocks V1 and V2 are compared as follows: V1 dominates V2 if every component of V1 is ≥ V2 and at least one is strictly greater; V2 dominates V1 if the reverse; otherwise they are concurrent. Concurrent writes mean neither causally preceded the other, and the system cannot pick one automatically without potentially losing data — so it presents both as siblings to the application. Vector clocks detect concurrency precisely, unlike LWW which silently resolves it. The cost is storage (vector size = number of replicas, growing over time) and application complexity (sibling handling). Production systems like Riak and Voldemort use vector clocks with periodic compaction (a "dot" mechanism) to bound size; DynamoDB and Cassandra prefer LWW for simplicity. The trade-off is correctness (vector clocks) versus operational simplicity (LWW).
**Visual:**
```
node A: vc=[a:1, b:0]  write x=1
node B: vc=[a:0, b:1]  write x=2   (concurrent, neither dominates)
compare: max(a:1,a:0)=1, max(b:0,b:1)=1, both strictly greater somewhere
        => concurrent => present both as siblings to app
node A: vc=[a:2, b:1] (after sync with B) -> next write dominates both
```

### Q4. What are CRDTs, and why are they suitable for offline-first applications?
**Answer:** A CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) is a data structure whose merge operation is associative, commutative, and idempotent — meaning any two replicas that have received the same set of updates, in any order, will converge to the same state without coordination or conflict resolution. Examples include G-Counter (grow-only counter), PN-Counter (positive-negative counter), G-Set (grow-only set), 2P-Set (add+remove via tombstones), OR-Set (observed-remove set), and sequence CRDTs like RGA and LSEQ used in collaborative editors. They are suitable for offline-first applications because they permit writes without coordination: a user on a plane can edit a document, the local CRDT records the operations, and on reconnect the operations merge deterministically with the server's state. There is no conflict to resolve and no data lost. The trade-offs are that CRDTs are domain-specific (you cannot make arbitrary structures CRDTs without redesign), some operations require tombstones (delete-then-add needs the delete to be remembered forever, or compaction rules must be defined), and metadata overhead can be significant (each operation may carry a unique id and vector). Yjs, Automerge, and Riak's CRDT module are the production-grade implementations.
**Visual:**
```
G-Counter on 3 replicas:
  A: {a:5, b:0, c:0}    B: {a:0, b:3, c:0}    C: {a:0, b:0, c:7}
merge: per-component max -> {a:5, b:3, c:7} = total 15 (deterministic)
order of merges does not matter (commutative + associative + idempotent)
```

### Q5. Compare read-repair, anti-entropy, and hinted handoff as propagation strategies.
**Answer:** Read-repair propagates divergence lazily during reads: the coordinator reads from multiple replicas, detects divergence, and writes the converged value back to lagging replicas. It is cheap (no background work) and self-correcting for hot keys, but cold keys can diverge indefinitely. Anti-entropy runs in the background: replicas periodically exchange Merkle trees of their key ranges and sync any differences; it catches all divergence eventually but consumes bandwidth and CPU even when nothing has changed. Hinted handoff handles temporary replica unavailability: if a replica is down when a write occurs, the coordinator stashes the write on another node with a hint, and the hint is forwarded to the original replica when it returns; it bridges the gap during partitions but does not catch divergence on available replicas. Production systems use all three in combination: hinted handoff for short outages, read-repair for hot keys, and scheduled anti-entropy (e.g., Cassandra's `nodetool repair` every 7 days) as a safety net. The trade-off is between latency of convergence (read-repair is fast for hot keys, anti-entropy is slow but comprehensive) and operational cost (anti-entropy scans everything, read-repair only touches what is read).
**Visual:**
```
read-repair     : on read -> detect divergence -> write back to laggards
anti-entropy    : background -> Merkle compare -> sync all differences
hinted handoff  : on write to down replica -> stash on alt -> forward later
(combine all three: hinted for outages, read-repair for hot keys,
 anti-entropy as periodic safety net)
```

### Q6. Why does DNS use eventual consistency, and what design lessons does it offer?
**Answer:** DNS is the longest-running eventually-consistent system on the planet, and its design choices are a masterclass in trading freshness for resilience. A DNS update propagates from the authoritative name server to recursive resolvers, each of which caches the record for the record's TTL (typically 300–86400 seconds). During the TTL window, a recursive resolver may serve a stale record even after the authoritative server has been updated. This is acceptable because DNS's primary invariant is availability — the internet must keep resolving names even when individual name servers fail — and the cost of staleness (a few minutes of stale A record after an IP change) is far lower than the cost of unavailability. The design lessons are: (1) make the convergence time an explicit, tunable parameter (TTL) rather than an emergent property; (2) accept a long convergence window if the cost of staleness is low and the cost of coordination is high; (3) layer caching aggressively — every layer (browser, OS, router, ISP recursive) caches, multiplying resilience; (4) keep the protocol simple and stateless so that any resolver can serve any query. Modern systems like DynamoDB and Cassandra apply these lessons through TTLs on cached reads and through deliberate acceptance of multi-second convergence windows.
**Visual:**
```
authoritative NS --update--> recursive resolver (caches for TTL)
                       \
                        v
TTL window: stale reads OK (cost of staleness < cost of coordination)
TTL expiry: resolver re-queries authoritative -> converges
design: availability > freshness; explicit convergence time; layer caching
```

### Q7. When is eventual consistency the wrong choice? Give three concrete anti-patterns.
**Answer:** Eventual consistency is the wrong choice whenever the cost of a stale read exceeds the cost of the coordination required for strong consistency. Three concrete anti-patterns: (1) Inventory counts for limited-stock items — two customers both see "1 left," both buy, one order must be cancelled, generating a customer-service incident and potential chargeback. The fix is strongly-consistent inventory checks (or a deterministic over-sell policy with documented business rules, like airlines overselling seats). (2) Lock acquisition and leader election — two processes both believe they hold a lock, both write to the resource they think they own, corrupting state. The fix is a strongly-consistent lock service (etcd, ZooKeeper, Chubby) or a fencing-token scheme. (3) Money movement — two concurrent withdrawals both read a $100 balance, both succeed, the account is now overdrawn by $100. The fix is linearizable transactions (Spanner, CockroachDB, or even a single-primary SQL database). The common thread is that these workloads have an invariant the system must preserve (no oversell, mutual exclusion, no negative balance) and that invariant is violated by any staleness. The architect's job is to identify these workloads and isolate them on strongly-consistent subsystems, while letting the rest of the system ride on eventual consistency.
**Visual:**
```
inventory:  2 customers see "1 left" -> 2 sales -> 1 cancellation  (BAD)
locks:      2 processes both hold lock -> 2 writers -> corruption   (BAD)
money:      2 withdrawals of $100 from $100 balance -> -$100        (BAD)
fix: linearizable subsystem for these; eventual for everything else
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix stores playback resume positions on Cassandra at `LOCAL_ONE` reads. A user pauses a movie on their phone, then opens the TV app, and the resume point is 30 seconds behind. Diagnose and propose a fix that preserves throughput.
**Answer:** The 30-second lag is the cross-region replication window for Cassandra `LOCAL_ONE` reads — the phone wrote to one Cassandra DC, the TV's read hit a different DC that has not yet received the write. The fix preserves throughput by adding session-level read-your-writes, not by raising the consistency level globally. The phone's pause event writes the resume position with a client-generated session token (a vector-clock or a monotonic sequence number); the TV's app, on launch, includes the session token in its read request, and the Cassandra coordinator (or a thin session layer in front) routes the read to a DC whose vector clock is at or beyond the session's — falling back to a `LOCAL_QUORUM` read across DCs only for that one request if no DC has caught up. This pattern keeps the global read path at `LOCAL_ONE` (cheap, fast) while guaranteeing the user sees their own latest write. The alternative — raising all reads to `LOCAL_QUORUM` — would double the read-unit cost and add cross-DC latency to every dashboard open, which is wasteful for a feature that only needs read-your-writes for the user's own data. The lesson is to layer session consistency on top of eventual consistency rather than globally escalating.
**Visual:**
```
phone pause -> write resume=12:30, session_vc=[u:101] -> DC:us-east
TV open    -> read resume, include session_vc=[u:101]
              coordinator routes to DC with vc >= [u:101]
              if us-east has it -> LOCAL_ONE (fast)
              if not -> fall back to LOCAL_QUORUM (one slow read)
```

### Q2. Instagram's like-counter on a viral post drops 5% of likes during peak traffic. Cassandra is configured with LWW on a single counter column. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** LWW on a single counter column is the wrong data model — concurrent like increments all read the current count, increment, and write back, and the LWW resolution drops every increment except the highest-timestamped one. The fix is to use Cassandra's native counter type (a CRDT-like PN-Counter) which keeps per-replica increments and sums them on read, so concurrent increments add rather than overwrite. If even the native counter is not fast enough for a viral post (Cassandra counters are famously fragile under heavy concurrent writes to the same partition), the production-grade pattern is to shard the counter across many partitions — `likes:post_42:shard_0` through `likes:post_42:shard_99` — have clients randomly pick a shard to increment, and sum all shards on read. This is the pattern Instagram and Facebook actually use for viral-content counters. The lesson is that LWW is appropriate for independent writes (last value wins) but catastrophically wrong for increments, which need a CRDT or a sharded accumulator. Always choose the data structure that matches the operation's algebra.
**Visual:**
```
WRONG (LWW on counter): 5 clients read count=100, write 101 -> LWW picks one 101
                          (4 increments LOST)
RIGHT (Cassandra counter): per-replica increments, summed on read -> 105
RIGHT (sharded counter):   likes:post:shard_{0..99} -> sum on read -> 105
                           (parallel writes, no contention)
```

### Q3. Amazon DynamoDB with `consistentRead=false` is used for a product catalog. A price update rolls out and 0.1% of reads return the old price for ~1 second. Is this acceptable? When would it not be?
**Answer:** For most product catalogs, 0.1% stale reads for ~1 second is acceptable — the cost is a tiny fraction of users seeing an old price briefly, and the savings in read-capacity units (eventual reads cost half as much as strongly-consistent reads) easily justify the risk. The catalog is mostly read-heavy and prices do not change frequently, so the convergence window is short and the business impact is minimal. It would not be acceptable in three cases: (1) flash sales with limited inventory, where the old price might be lower than the new price and customers could buy at the old price before the update propagates, losing revenue; (2) regulated industries like pharmaceuticals or financial products, where displaying the wrong price could violate consumer-protection laws; (3) price changes that trigger automated systems — if a repricing engine reads its own price to decide the next price, staleness creates a feedback loop. The fix in those cases is to use `consistentRead=true` for the specific reads that need freshness, or to add a version-stamp layer where the catalog write returns a version and subsequent reads include `?if-version>=N`. The default eventual reads stay cheap; the freshness-critical reads pay the extra cost.
**Visual:**
```
default catalog reads:  consistentRead=false (cheap, 0.1% briefly stale) OK
flash sale:             consistentRead=true on price + inventory  (correctness)
regulated products:     consistentRead=true on price  (compliance)
repricing feedback:     consistentRead=true OR version-stamp (avoid loop)
```

### Q4. You design a chat application on DynamoDB. Two users in different regions send messages to the same group chat concurrently. How do you ensure both messages are preserved in the correct causal order?
**Answer:** DynamoDB's default LWW on the same partition key would drop one of the two concurrent messages — so the schema must avoid collisions on the same partition. The pattern is to use a composite partition key that includes a per-message unique identifier, like `(group_id, message_id)` where `message_id` is a UUID or a snowflake timestamp, so each message is its own row and concurrent writes never collide. To preserve causal order on read, each message carries a `parent_message_id` (or a vector clock for full causal tracking) and the client reconstructs the conversation order by topologically sorting on read. If the group is small enough, store all messages in a single DynamoDB item as a list attribute, use a conditional update with `attribute_not_exists(message_id)` to prevent collisions, and accept that all writes serialize through one item — fine for groups under a few thousand messages but not for large public channels. For large channels, partition the conversation by time windows (`group_id#2025-01-15`) and use parallel query + merge on read. The underlying principle: never let concurrent writes collide on the same key — disperse them by unique id, then reconstruct order at read time using causal metadata stored alongside the message.
**Visual:**
```
WRONG: same partition key -> LWW drops one message
RIGHT: partition = group_id#message_id (unique per message)
       each message row: {msg_id, parent_msg_id, text, ts}
       read: query group_id, topologically sort by parent_msg_id
       (causal order preserved, concurrent writes never collide)
```

### Q5. Cassandra cluster experiences disk pressure from growing tombstones after a deployment that deletes many rows. Explain the phenomenon and prescribe a remediation.
**Answer:** Tombstones are deletion markers that Cassandra writes instead of physically removing data, because in an eventually-consistent system a physical delete could be resurrected by a lagging replica that did not see the delete. The deployment that deleted many rows generated a large number of tombstones, and now every read of the affected partitions must scan past them, increasing read latency and disk usage. The remediation has two layers. First, run `nodetool compaction` to trigger the compaction process that physically removes tombstones older than `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) — this reclaims disk and speeds reads. Second, address the root cause: avoid deletes where possible by using TTLs (rows that auto-expire), use immutable append-only schemas where deletes are not needed, and tune `tombstone_warn_threshold` and `tombstone_failure_threshold` to alert before reads are impacted. For the immediate deployment, the SRE should run a major compaction on the affected keyspaces during a low-traffic window, monitor disk and read-latency recovery, and add a tombstone-growth alert to the dashboard. Long-term, the schema should be redesigned to favor TTLs over explicit deletes wherever the data has a natural expiration.
**Visual:**
```
delete row -> writes tombstone (marker, not physical delete)
                -> read must skip tombstones (latency, disk)
                -> compaction removes tombstones older than gc_grace_seconds
remediation: nodetool compaction (immediate)
             + TTLs instead of deletes (long-term)
             + alert on tombstone count per read
```

### Q6. You build a collaborative whiteboard app for offline-first mobile. Multiple users edit the same shape offline; on reconnect, conflicts must merge without data loss. Which eventual-consistency strategy do you choose and why?
**Answer:** Use CRDTs, specifically an operation-based CRDT for the shape graph where each operation (add shape, move shape, delete shape, recolor) is uniquely identified, commutes with concurrent operations, and is idempotent. The reason CRDTs are right and LWW/vector-clocks are wrong: LWW would silently drop one user's edits; vector clocks would detect the conflict but require application-side merge logic that is hard to get right for spatial operations; CRDTs guarantee automatic deterministic merge. For shape moves, use an LWW-Register per shape property (last move wins, with timestamps from a hybrid logical clock to handle clock skew); for shape adds, use a G-Set (grow-only, never collide); for deletes, use an OR-Set (observed-remove: a delete only removes the shape that existed at delete time, so concurrent re-adds survive); for color/size, use per-property LWW registers. The library Yjs or Automerge provides these primitives. On reconnect, the client exchanges its operation log with the server, both sides apply the merge function, and convergence is guaranteed without application conflict resolution. The trade-off is metadata overhead — each shape carries a unique id and operation log — but for a whiteboard this is acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
user A (offline): move shape S to (10,10), color=red
user B (offline): move shape S to (20,20), color=blue
reconnect: CRDT merge
  position: LWW-Register -> picks higher-timestamp move
  color:    LWW-Register -> picks higher-timestamp color
  (no data loss, deterministic, no app conflict logic)
library: Yjs / Automerge (production-grade CRDTs)
```

### Q7. A Kafka consumer group rebalances during a partition, and a consumer that was processing a message is kicked out. The message is re-delivered to another consumer. How does the system remain correct without double-processing?
**Answer:** Kafka's at-least-once delivery means the new consumer will receive the message that the old consumer was processing; if the old consumer completed the side effect but did not commit the offset before being kicked out, the side effect will execute twice. The fix is to make every side-effect operation idempotent so that duplicate delivery is safe. The standard pattern: each message carries a unique id (Kafka's producer idempotence provides this for produce-side, but consumers must add it for processing-side), and the consumer writes the id to a dedupe table (a Redis SET or a database unique constraint) before performing the side effect. If the id is already in the dedupe table, the consumer skips the side effect and commits the offset. For exactly-once semantics within Kafka itself, use the transactions API: the consumer's offset commit and the producer's output to a downstream topic are wrapped in a single transaction, so they either both commit or both abort. For exactly-once to an external system (a database write), the dedupe table must live in the same database as the side effect so they commit atomically. The general lesson: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing equals effectively-once semantics, and this is the right mental model for almost all real-world stream processing.
**Visual:**
```
consumer-1: receive msg(id=42) -> process -> (kicked before commit)
consumer-2: receive msg(id=42) -> check dedupe table
            if id=42 exists -> skip, commit offset
            if not -> write to dedupe table + side effect (atomic), commit
exactly-once within Kafka: transactions API (offset commit + produce atomic)
effectively-once to external: dedupe table in same DB as side effect
```
